Paper: Atta et al. (2023)
Critical caveat for synthesis: Raw rice husk; no real-water, regeneration or column study. qmax = 2.47 mg/g. Isotherm dose about 90 g/L, which affects practical comparability.
Action required: Check values against full text; preserve high-dose limitation in synthesis.

Paper: Alidadi et al. (2018)
Critical caveat for synthesis: Hospital-sample tetracycline decreased from 0.25 mg/L to below HPLC detection. Single-stage desorption/regeneration only; reuse cycles not established.
Action required: Verify exact methods and whether the hospital-sample result is described accurately.

Paper: Delmond et al. (2023)
Critical caveat for synthesis: Table 3 prints modified-ash Langmuir qmax = 12,179.5 mg/g, which is physically implausible versus measured modified-ash capacities around 2.79–3.58 mg/g in the column tests and roughly 4 mg/g in batch figures. The study tests model solutions at 30–150 mg/L for isotherms and uses 100 mg/L in the main filtration comparison, far above cited treated-effluent concentrations. The estimate that 1 g can treat ~330 L at 0.0085 mg/L is extrapolated, not experimentally validated. Chemical modification uses sequential H3PO4, H2SO4 and KOH/ethanol treatments plus substantial washing; no measured cost, regeneration cost, or LCA is provided.
Action required: Do not use the 12,179.5 mg/g fitted qmax as a valid capacity unless resolved against the original data/correction. Keep observed 2.79–4.76 mg/g capacities and removal percentages separate from the fitted parameter. Label low-concentration treated-volume calculations as projections, not demonstrations. Discuss chemical/wash burdens and the proposed thermal end-of-life route without claiming verified economic or environmental superiority.

Paper: Conde-Cid et al. (2021)
Critical caveat for synthesis: No reliable Langmuir qmax: study fits Linear and Freundlich models only. Contact pH was measured but not adjusted/buffered. Material doses are unequal (pine bark/oak ash 50 g/L; mussel shell 400 g/L). Source-text inconsistencies: abstract says C0 starts at 1 µmol/L while Methods lists 2.5–50 µmol/L; abstract says oak-ash adsorption <45% while Results text says <40%; mussel-shell adsorption is described as <15% in some passages but <10% later. Pine bark shows <11% desorption, but this is not multi-cycle regeneration. Supplementary information is absent from the uploaded PDF, and real-water, column, cost/LCA data are not reported.
Action required: Preserve original-source discrepancy in the batch note; if using percentages, quote the relevant passage or digitize Fig. 2 rather than choosing one unsupported threshold. Keep observed µmol/kg uptake distinct from fitted Kd/KF; disclose unbuffered pH and unequal doses. Do not claim qmax, operational regeneration, real-water validation or economic superiority.

Paper: Míguez-González et al. (2023)
Critical caveat for synthesis: The study tests individual antibiotics at 25–600 µmol/L in 10 mL against 0.5 g sorbent. Table 1 fitted Langmuir qmax values are error-prone for several pairs; TMP/pine bark qmax = 76,429 µmol/kg has very large error (~4.6×10⁴ µmol/kg), while maximum mass-balance uptake at 600 µmol/L is only 12,000 µmol/kg. The authors state saturation may not have been achieved and CIP/pine bark could not be modelled because removal was 100% across tested levels. Do not equate the abstract's approximate observed capacities with fitted qmax. The study's main application is retention in agricultural soils, not wastewater treatment validation. Supplementary material containing sorbent physicochemistry was not supplied.
Action required: Separate observed retention percentage/uptake from fitted qmax; do not use unstable qmax values as cross-study rankings. Report model errors and state that no saturation may have been achieved. Classify the work primarily as soil/side-stream retention evidence rather than a demonstrated wastewater unit process; check the supplementary material before detailed mechanism or material-property claims.

Paper: Li et al. (2019)
Critical caveat for synthesis: The paper studies TMP and diclofenac (DCF); DCF is an NSAID, not an antibiotic. The rendered PDF tables show Qe and Langmuir Qm in µg/g and concentration axes in µg/L; some PDF text/OCR extraction renders µ as m, which would inflate capacities by 1000× if misread. Kinetic tests use C0=500 µg/L, while isotherm ranges are much higher and differ by material (TMP macro-algae figure extends to 400,000 µg/L). Capacity units/conditions are not harmonized across kinetic and isotherm experiments.
Action required: Include TMP only in antibiotic-specific counts; retain source values in µg/g and explicitly convert to mg/g (divide by 1000) only when needed. Verify units from the rendered tables/Fig. 4 rather than OCR text. Do not compare fitted isotherm Qm directly against observed low-concentration kinetic uptake; state that concentration ranges differ markedly.

Paper: Yao et al. (2023) — Fe/N co-doped rape-straw biochar
Critical caveat for synthesis: Langmuir qmax values are model-derived at 298–318 K (CIP 25.36–46.45 mg/g; Cu2+ 27.92–30.77 mg/g); binary qmax lower (CIP 18.84, Cu2+ 17.23 mg/g at 318 K). Paper: Jaria et al. (2019) — waste-derived GAC fixed bed
Critical caveat for synthesis: Only sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is an antibiotic target; carbamazepine and paroxetine are non-antibiotic comparators. Experimental curve-integrated qtotal can differ sharply from fitted Thomas/Yan q values; authors note several fitted capacities overestimate measured capacities, and curves did not reach C/C0=1 within test window.
Action required: Use SMX only in antibiotic-specific comparisons. Keep observed integrated qtotal distinct from qTH/qY and from a true saturation capacity. Record real WWTP-effluent feed as filtered and spiked, with target background below detection.

Paper: Gao et al. (2024) — KOH-activated dyeing-sludge biochar
Critical caveat for synthesis: Main text inconsistencies: SBET is 1178.4 m2/g in abstract/characterization/Table 2 but 1078.4 in one discussion sentence; Eq. (2) writes R%=(C0−Ct)/Ct×100, unlike the conventional denominator C0; isotherm method says 298 K but conclusion states qmax at 278 K; fixed-bed max 1124.2 mg/g exceeds batch Langmuir qmax 1081.3 mg/g; abstract/body label cycle-5 metrics differently (86.35% removal vs 86.88% regeneration efficiency and 86.35% retained capacity). Batch dose and real tailwater details are incomplete in the supplied main PDF.

Use 1178.4 m2/g only with a note that one in-text sentence prints 1078.4; flag the formula and capacity/temperature/regeneration discrepancies for SI/author verification. Treat ~$9/kg as an author-reported preliminary preparation estimate, not complete TEA/LCA; include Fenton chemical demand and spent-liquid considerations.

Paper: Jiao et al. (2024) — OTC molecularly imprinted magnetic biochar
Critical caveat for synthesis: Abstract/narrative report MBC qmax 38.84 mg/g but Table 2 gives 38.34 mg/g. Abstract gives 299 K while most methods say 25 °C. Main PDF specifies an iron-leaching test but supplies no numeric result in the accessible body. PSO fit is described as chemisorption, which is not proved by fit alone. Fig. 4a also reports OTC uptake 11.97 mg/g while its caption states 4 mg/L feed and 0.5 g/L adsorbent, implying a mass-balance ceiling of 8 mg/g even at complete removal; this value exceeds the stated ceiling.

Search SI independently; user is not expected to provide SI. Resolve the Fig. 4a capacity/condition mismatch before using 11.97 mg/g; retain selectivity-factor evidence separately from this suspect uptake value.

Paper: Mosaffa et al. (2024) — bacterial-cellulose-char / CS-PEI beads
Critical caveat for synthesis: The article reports empirical q values 960.778 mg/g TET and 691.325 mg/g MET at 400 mg/L initial concentration (~0.267 g/L dose). Paper: Masrura et al. (2024) — solvent-modified sludge biochar for human urine

Paper: Hacıosmanoğlu et al. (2022) — review of natural/modified clay minerals
Critical caveat for synthesis: Review has 82 selected articles and summarizes many capacities, but key tables are in referenced supplementary Tables S1–S6 not included in uploaded main PDF. Paper: Wang et al. (2010) — ciprofloxacin on Ca-montmorillonite SAz-1

Paper: Usama et al. (2025) — PET-derived KOH activated carbon kC1170

Paper: Fraiha et al. (2024) — clay/pharmaceutical adsorption review
Critical caveat for synthesis: Review Table 2 compiles mixed pharmaceutical targets and different test conditions, often with missing fields; the review concerns pharmaceuticals generally, not antibiotics only. The main PDF does not provide a reproducible systematic-search strategy/flow.
Action required: Use as narrative secondary source and citation-discovery only. Check original studies before entering capacities/removal percentages into quantitative synthesis. Do not claim the review is systematic or use its summary table as a homogeneous material ranking.

Paper: Yaqubi et al. (2021) — leached carbon-black waste and chitosan beads
Critical caveat for synthesis: Results text reports LCBW BET ~375 m²/g while conclusion reports ~275 m²/g. Action required: Keep both BET values and the dosage ambiguity visible. Do not promote fitted fixed-bed q to a validated dynamic capacity. No unit cost, within-study regeneration study, or full LCA; residual metal fate needs cautious discussion.

Paper: Zhu et al. (2024) — in-situ N-doped biochar from oxytetracycline fermentation residue
Critical caveat for synthesis: Printed methods equations use (Ce−C0) in qe and removal formulas, appearing to reverse signs for adsorption when Ce<C0. Main text reports 4% decline after five reuse cycles but Table 1 gives target-specific reusability percentages 96.90, 89.23, 95.08 and 95.44 without fully clear cycle mapping. SI Tables S1–S7/Figs. S1–S4 are unavailable in the uploaded PDF; no full cost/yield/energy or real wastewater data.
Action required: Flag the equation as a likely printed sign error; do not reproduce incorrectly. Keep capacity values as abstract/conclusion-reported Langmuir Qmax pending SI parameters. Report no leaching/four-gene signal only under the described assays; do not generalize to all genes/matrices or claim universal safety.

Paper: Yan et al. (2024) — review of tetracycline adsorption by biochar
Critical caveat for synthesis: Review Table 1 and real-water/regeneration sections compile primary papers with different feedstocks, concentration, pH, dose, models and matrices. Values in the review are secondary and may mix reported maxima/observed results; TOC reduction examples are not target-specific tetracycline removal.
Action required: Use for taxonomy, gaps and citation mining. Trace any quantitative claim to original paper and preserve its exact test conditions and metric; never count a review-table value as an independent experimental result.

Paper: Zango et al. (2024) — systematic review of biomass biochar/AC for antibiotic wastewater
Critical caveat for synthesis: Search ended 2024-04-30. Fig. 1 reports 305 full texts included in qualitative assessment and 162 studies included in SLR, while full-text exclusions are 54 and narrative later refers to 301 papers considered. The displayed Scopus/WoS Boolean search string lacks explicit parentheses around OR. Table 4 contains price estimates from different years and locations.
Action required: Keep search counts as author-reported with an internal discrepancy flag until clarified. Do not describe it as current 2026 evidence or use the cost table as a current comparable price list. Use citations to prioritize primary-paper screening.

Paper: Sumariva et al. (2024) — Esquivias clay honeycomb monoliths
Critical caveat for synthesis: Clay powder capacities and monolith recirculation removals use different test setups and cannot be ranked directly. Monolith tests use high TC levels (~231–460 mg/L) and recirculation, not a once-through trace-level wastewater pilot. TC UV–Vis spectra shift with pH (λmax 356/358/375 nm at pH 3/7/9), and higher temperature/light/air can form transformation products. Post-use heating at 300–350 °C is a separate proposed regeneration/destruction step, not adsorption.
Action required: Keep powder mg/g, monolith % removal and recirculation flow/time separate. Preserve pH-specific analytical calibration and flag TC transformation. Do not claim full mineralization from H2O/CO2 TPO signals alone; no detailed TEA/LCA.

Paper: Nugraha et al. (2025) — adsorption technology for hospital wastewater review
Critical caveat for synthesis: Review's broad 70–90% adsorption range compiles heterogeneous studies. Examples include naturally occurring HWW, HWW spiked at 10 mg/L, and municipal wastewater connected to hospitals; these are materially different matrices. Only PAC/GAC are described as implemented at full scale; most advanced adsorbents remain lab-scale. Supplementary Tables S1–S6 not included in uploaded main PDF.
Action required: Use for hospital-specific background and citation chasing, not as a homogeneous performance benchmark. Check each primary study for water matrix, C0, dose, adsorbent and treatment-train role before quantitative use.

Paper: Sousa et al. (2026) — fixed-bed brewery-spent-grain biochar and LCA
Critical caveat for synthesis: Real WWTP effluent was 0.45 μm filtered and autoclaved before adsorption tests. Flow, matrix and ternary antibiotic feed strongly changed breakthrough. Microwave regeneration at 600 °C was demonstrated over two cycles for TMP only; reported 118%/146% regeneration efficiency means q_regenerated/q_initial, not percentage of antibiotic desorbed. LCA totals are in SI Table S4, unavailable in uploaded main PDF, and LCA is lab-scale adsorbent production rather than cradle-to-grave operation.
Action required: Label matrix and all conditions. Do not generalize TMP regeneration results to SMX/CIP. Report relative LCA hotspots only unless totals/functional boundary are verified; do not claim full-life-cycle superiority.

Paper: Kar et al. (2025) — wood-apple-shell ACNB for enrofloxacin
Critical caveat for synthesis: Paper reports dose ranges inconsistently (abstract 0.2–1 g/L, methods 0.45–1.5 g/L, results optimum 2 g/L). The “activated N-biochar” preparation describes H3PO4 activation without an external N-doping step and reports N 0.12 wt%. Table 3 prints micropore volume 1.76 cm3/g; production yield/mass basis is not reported. Table 4 lists ΔG° about −3825 to −4089 kJ/mol with ΔH° −0.735 kJ/mol and ΔS° −0.107 kJ/(mol K), inconsistent with the stated ΔG=ΔH−TΔS relation. DNA-ethidium-bromide fluorescence assay does not establish overall real-wastewater ecotoxicological safety.
Action required: Keep the material term as author terminology, not as intentional N doping. Do not use ΔG values or the 16.7-times cost claim quantitatively before resolving arithmetic, yield/mass basis and cost boundary; do not claim treated water universally safe from fluorescence results. Report Qmax 54.94 mg/g and 96.5% as author-reported with their conditions.

Paper: Sompornpailin et al. (2024) — GAC and ARG/ARB in secondary hospital effluent
Critical caveat for synthesis: Single-solute conditions and mixed-solute results differ substantially; MEM and paper-labelled SMZ were outcompeted/not adsorbed in six-antibiotic mixture. GAC column lowered many ARGs in effluent but some microbial taxa/genes accumulated in used GAC. Bacterial-toxicity conclusion comes from E. coli growth assay, not a broad toxicity panel. SI tables with intermediate identities/gene abundances are not included in upload.
Action required: Keep low-microgram/L Kp/isotherm study separate from high-mg/L qmax studies. Do not equate removal from water with destruction/safe disposal. Treat spent GAC as potentially infectious/resistome-bearing and preserve SMZ label unless the target identity is verified.

Paper: Al-sareji et al. (2024) — banana-peel activated carbon for amoxicillin/carbamazepine
Critical caveat for synthesis: Study combines amoxicillin and carbamazepine; carbamazepine is not an antibiotic. Initial mixture concentration basis is not fully explicit in extracted procedure. Seven-cycle removal falls strongly in lake water and wastewater (cycle 7 amoxicillin/carbamazepine 25.43/15.84% lake, 20.43/12.09% wastewater). Water matrix characterization points to an earlier study. No numerical production cost, yield or full LCA is reported.
Action required: Only include amoxicillin in antibiotic-only quantitative synthesis; label carbamazepine a co-contaminant. Preserve mixture/test conditions and real-water cycle decline. Do not use sustainable/cost-effective as though a numerical TEA/LCA were performed.

Paper: Alidadi et al. (2018) — Fe-modified sawdust for tetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: RSM-predicted optimum is 98.40% at 12.5 mg/L, pH 7.9, dose 4.8 g/L and 118.3 min; listed validation runs reached up to 92.37%, and do not reproduce the exact predicted point. Real hospital-water TC fell from 0.25 mg/L to below HPLC detection, but the report does not give a numeric LOD/LOQ. The paper reports single-stage regeneration only and calculates 88% water reclaimed from the adsorption/desorption volume balance.
Action required: Keep model prediction separate from measured validation and below-detection separate from zero. Do not relabel 88% as antibiotic desorption or multicycle regeneration. Costs/impact and Fe leaching are not quantified; authors identify synthetic/real feed concentration mismatch as a limitation.

Paper: García-Criado et al. (2025) — purified stevensite for tetracyclines/metabolites
Critical caveat for synthesis: Concentration inconsistency: abstract reports 5 mg/L, methods generally 2 mg/L, and one kinetics passage appears to say 2 mg/mL. Kinetic results claim qe experimental ~0.98–1.58 mg/g and near-complete removal in minutes, whereas narrative qmax includes >200,000 mg/g (called TC in one section/TGC in conclusion); Table 2 gives 86.1–1000 mg/g, with multiple values exactly 1000. Extreme pH can degrade some analytes, salinity can reduce OTC adsorption by ~50%, and reuse uses buffer/acetone regenerant. Real-water trials are spiked to 2 mg/L.
Action required: Do not include the >200,000 mg/g claim as a valid capacity. Prefer direct qe, removal and time with explicit feed conditions; flag Table 2 fitted qmax until clarified. Separate adsorption from potential analyte degradation at extreme pH, and spiked matrices from native wastewater.

Paper: Li et al. (2026) — ammonia-assisted ball-milled N-doped biochar for tetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: Abstract says total pore volume 276 cm3/g, while main text states 0.2951 cm3/g (with micropore volume 0.03822 cm3/g); this is a source error. The synthesis includes 700 °C pyrolysis for 2 h and 300 rpm ball milling for 24 h, but no quantified electricity, cost or LCA. First-cycle removal is 95.6%, but regeneration declines to 54.6% in cycle 2 and 40.6% in cycle 6. Mechanism narrative describes PSO as chemisorption-controlled while FTIR/thermodynamics also support multiple noncovalent interactions.
Action required: Use the detailed main-text pore volume, flag abstract discrepancy, and label Qm as model-fitted. Do not call the material cost-effective based on a quantitative TEA because none is reported; prominently report the poor multicycle retention.

Paper: Atta et al. (2023) — raw rice husk for levofloxacin
Critical caveat for synthesis: The study reports a Langmuir qmax of 2.47 mg/g and tests rice-husk doses from 5 to 120 g/L; reported dose sweep removal rises 27.8% to 93.8%. Paper has no real-water tests, regeneration, empirical unit cost or LCA.
Action required: Keep fitted qmax separate from percent removal; emphasize the very high doses. Do not call the material cost-effective from the authors' low-cost description alone.

Action required: Use as a secondary narrative source only. Do not count the review’s tables as independent experiments; verify primary references for numerical capacities and exclude oxidative/photocatalytic degradation values from adsorption-only synthesis.

Paper: Yin et al. (2024) — UiO-66/CNT electroactive nanofiltration membrane
Critical caveat for synthesis: Primary metrics are membrane rejection/permeance (e.g. 99.3% TC rejection), not adsorbed mass per unit adsorbent. Electric self-cleaning uses ROS-mediated degradation of foulants. Process-cost comparisons are membrane-specific and are not directly comparable with adsorbent unit cost.
Action required: Exclude from the core adsorption-capacity matrix. Use only as adjacent membrane-technology context if needed; do not convert rejection % to mg/g or classify self-cleaning degradation as adsorption.

Paper: Li et al. (2024) — magnetic biochar for antibiotic removal review
Critical caveat for synthesis: Review abstract compiles MBC capacities from 5 to 900 mg/g and states removal commonly exceeds 90% in 60 min, but underlying studies vary in antibiotic, C0, adsorbent dose, preparation, fitted/observed metric and conditions. Review discusses adsorption and catalytic degradation in separate tables/sections. Mechanisms are acknowledged as partly ambiguous; preparation costs and secondary pollution remain concerns.
Action required: Use as secondary synthesis for MBC processing routes, hypotheses and risk themes. Do not count review entries as independent primary experiments, treat the broad range as normalized performance, or mix catalytic-degradation values with adsorption capacity. Verify numerical claims and regeneration examples against primary sources.

Paper: Jia et al. (2024) — biochar-based antibiotic removal review
Critical caveat for synthesis: Reported maximum capacities of 0.3–612.2 mg/g compile heterogeneous conditions (cited antibiotic concentrations 0.003–200 mg/L). The article covers both adsorption and biodegradation/biotic roles and discusses ARG-related outcomes and engineering configurations; these are different endpoints and not interchangeable.
Action required: Use for secondary mechanistic, solution-chemistry, biotic and engineering context. Trace quantitative performance to cited primary papers. Distinguish sorption from biotransformation, and treat relative cost rankings or engineering benefits as contextual rather than universal without process-specific costing.

Paper: Gopal & Mukherjee (2024) — Fe/Cu CNS alginate–CMC–chitosan beads for norfloxacin
Critical caveat for synthesis: The study reports about 86% NOR removal and Langmuir qmax 354.9±41 mg/g, but sorbent concentration/dose statements vary among abstract, methods and figure captions. Kinetic-table qe(cal) estimates differ (PFO 107.339 mg/g; PSO 200 mg/g), and the PSO estimate exceeds the simple mass-balance ceiling if the stated 0.15 g/L dose applies at 20 mg/L initial concentration. The UV–vis method reports LOD 2.72 mg/L and LOQ 8.24 mg/L; 86% removal from 20 mg/L implies a residual near 2.8 mg/L, below stated LOQ. TOC/LC-MS evidence indicates catalytic transformation contributes, so removal is not adsorption alone. Natural-water samples were spiked at 20 mg/L and showed only ~24–28% removal; simulated hospital effluent is not untreated native wastewater. Reported humic-acid/microplastic units and thermodynamic table values warrant checking.
Action required: Separate fitted qmax, model-derived qe and actual observed uptake; resolve dose units and confirm residual quantification against LOD/LOQ/ESI. Treat this as a combined adsorption/degradation composite, not a pure adsorption-only result. Label 20 mg/L matrix-spike results as high-concentration tests; do not claim trace-level field efficacy or quantified sustainability.

Paper: Shaha et al. (2025) — sulfonated graphene oxide for ciprofloxacin
Critical caveat for synthesis: Fitted Langmuir qm is reported as 1,000 μmol/g (331.35 mg/g) in Table 2 (printed p. 40825); Fig. 10 (printed p. 40824) states the fitted isotherm data span 50–1000 μmol/L at 0.2 g/L, while the separate kinetic/concentration series in Table 1 is 10–100 μmol/L. The earlier simple ceiling of 500 μmol/g based on 100 μmol/L was therefore applied to the wrong series and must not be used to disqualify q_m. Do keep the source inconsistencies visible: Table 1 gives 237.12 μmol/g at 50 μmol/L while the reuse section says 239.39 μmol/g as the initial/direct uptake; the text reports 96.53% removal at 25 °C though qe=237.12 μmol/g, 50 μmol/L and 0.2 g/L imply about 94.85% by the paper's mass-balance equation. Regeneration uses 1 M HCl in DMF; synthesis uses concentrated acids, KMnO4, HCl and organic solvents. Only duplicate measurements are stated; no real-water validation, cost or LCA is reported.
Action required: Keep observed qe, reported removal percentage and fitted q_m separate. Preserve the Table 1/reuse qe difference and the qe/removal mass-balance discrepancy without recalculating the source data in place. Use the isotherm-specific range (50–1000 μmol/L) when describing the fit; do not apply the separate 10–100 μmol/L kinetic range as its loading ceiling. Retain cost/energy and real-water-validation caveats.

Paper: Adu-Poku et al. (2024) — acid-activated coconut-husk biochar for amoxicillin
Critical caveat for synthesis: The abstract gives initial AMX concentrations of 0.5–2.5 mg/L, whereas Methods/Results describe 20–70 mg/L and a typical test at 50 mg/L. The paper reports experimental kinetic qe=245.9±1.4 mg/g and Langmuir qmax=239.23 mg/g, but if the stated typical batch condition is 25 mg adsorbent in 50 mL at 50 mg/L, mass balance limits uptake to 100 mg/g. qmax is also slightly below the reported experimental qe. Figure 10 (20–70 mg/L) gives plotted uptake up to about 136 mg/g, closer to the stated mass balance at 70 mg/L. Four-cycle description of a near-20% loss conflicts with a first-cycle removal of 98.6% and fourth-cycle removal reported as 72.2%. BET area/pore metrics, product yield, cost and LCA are not reported.
Action required: Do not use 245.9 mg/g as a verified capacity or merge it with Fig. 10 plotted results until the exact kinetic conditions/raw data are clarified. Keep both abstract and methods concentration ranges visible in notes. Report the regeneration results with the source's conflicting wording; label tests as synthetic/artificially polluted water.

Paper: Li et al. (2025) — PGOT@GEL graphene oxide-based hydrogel for CIP/GAT and Cu²⁺
Critical caveat for synthesis: PGOT@GEL uses multi-step GO oxidation, phosphorus doping, TETA grafting, β-cyclodextrin modification and AMPS polymerization. Reported fitted qmax values are 821.24 mg/g CIP and 755.96 mg/g GAT; RSM validation uses 296.52 mg/L CIP, not trace environmental concentration. Real-water results are stated as >89% removal across four conditions, but key matrix/spike details are in supplementary information not supplied here. Seven-cycle reuse requires 12 h methanol soaking after each adsorption. Synthesis/reuse chemical use, solvent recovery, waste handling, cost and LCA are not quantified.
Action required: Separate fitted qmax, RSM-optimized uptake, and pH-test uptake/removal. Do not generalize high-concentration RSM or incompletely described water-matrix results to trace-level wastewater. Discuss methanol regeneration and the multi-step synthesis as uncosted processing burdens; verify matrix conditions from the supporting information before calling the data untreated-real-water validation.

Paper: Cuevas et al. (2019) — mineral sorbents for tetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: The batch tests cover pH 4, 6, 8 and initial TC 33.2–1176.5 mg/L, with 0.1 M NaCl at 25 °C. Even the lowest concentration (33.2 mg/L = 33,200 µg/L) is much higher than the typical effluent level <1 µg/L cited in the introduction. The highest observed uptake for LC montmorillonite (381.2 mg/g) is at 1176.5 mg/L and cannot be presented as demonstrated trace-level performance. Table 4 reports Langmuir Cm in cmol/kg rather than mg/g; some Cm values are far above CEC, and the paper notes anomalous/near-linear fit behavior for some mineral–pH combinations. No real wastewater, regeneration, fixed-bed, process-cost or life-cycle results are reported.
Action required: Keep observed uptake at each stated C0 separate from fitted parameters. Do not convert Cm to mg/g without explicit stoichiometric justification; flag values exceeding CEC or associated with near-linear fits. Describe 'low concentration' only relative to the study's test range, and state there is no trace-level or real-wastewater validation.

Paper: Abd El-Monaem et al. (2022) — chitosan-composite antibiotic adsorption review
Critical caveat for synthesis: This is a narrative review, not a primary experiment. Tables 2–7 compile qmax, pH and removal summaries from heterogeneous cited studies using different concentrations, adsorbent dosages, matrices and model conventions. Some discussed systems have transformation processes as well as sorption; for example, the review's Cs-Fe/Ni account for amoxicillin includes reductive β-lactam cleavage. Several very high review-reported capacities (e.g., 1111 mg/g for MgO/Cs/GO and 1000 mg/g for NOR on MgO/Cs/GO) require tracing to the original experiment and checking its units/mass balance.
Action required: Use this paper for taxonomy and literature discovery, not as an independent primary-data point or stand-alone performance ranking. Verify capacities, endpoints, dose/concentration and mechanisms against primary papers; separate adsorption from degradation/combined removal and avoid comparing compiled qmax values across unlike conditions.

Paper: Mirizadeh et al. (2025) — chitosan-based adsorbents for antibiotic removal, batch and dynamic review
Critical caveat for synthesis: This is a systematic review, not a primary experiment. It reports 74 included papers (59 batch, 15 dynamic) and uses an exclusion criterion based on journals with impact factor <3. Its Tables 1–6 compile studies with highly heterogeneous concentrations, dosage, pH, column geometry, flow rates, endpoint definitions and model conventions. Fixed-bed q0/breakthrough data are not equivalent to batch qmax or qe. The review's general claim that PSO fit is consistent with chemisorption should not be treated as direct mechanistic proof.
Action required: Use for citation discovery and for mapping the under-represented dynamic/fixed-bed literature. Trace selected qmax, qe, q0, breakthrough and mechanistic statements to primary sources. Keep batch and column metrics in separate table fields and document the review's journal-impact-factor exclusion criterion.

Paper: Mohammed-Ridha & Abdul-ahad (2014) — levofloxacin adsorption on barley husks and eggshells
Critical caveat for synthesis: Uploaded filename contains '(2023)' but the article imprint is Journal of Engineering Vol. 20, No. 12, December 2014. Study uses a commercial levofloxacin tablet rather than clearly documented pure standard. Table 2 reports fitted Langmuir qm for barley husks 125.735 mg/g despite maximum experimentally accessible loading of 30 mg/g at C0=150 mg/L, 100 mL and 0.5 g sorbent. For the separate 1 L, 150 mg/L kinetic setup, doses are stated as 20.745 g AC, 30.722 g barley husks and 720 g eggshells, but Table 3 kinetic qe values greatly exceed some dose-specific mass-balance ceilings (maximum about 6.87, 4.64 and 0.198 mg/g respectively at Ce/C0=0.05). The table's PFO and PSO qe values diverge sharply.
Action required: Retain the publication year as 2014, not the file name's 2023. Keep observed removal (71% barley at 5 g/L) separate from fitted qm and kinetic parameters. Do not use the disputed 125.735 mg/g fitted capacity or inconsistent Table 3 qe figures in rankings until exact conditions/table errors are resolved. Note that the tests use synthetic, high-concentration solutions and eggshell dosage was tenfold higher than barley/AC in the headline comparison.

Paper: Hamdi et al. (2024) — tetracycline adsorption/desorption on raw and activated Tunisian clays
Critical caveat for synthesis: The study tests C0=25–1000 µmol/L (roughly 11–444 mg/L TC) with 0.5 g clay per 10 mL and 0.005 M CaCl2 for 24 h. Even high reported removal near 100% is not trace-level wastewater validation. The paper reports very high raw-clay EC (446–495 dS/m); preserve the published units and verify before reinterpreting them. Activation uses 5% Na2CO3 at 75°C for 1 h or 3 N HCl at 75°C for 4 h (acid-treated clays require washing and drying), yet authors conclude activation is unnecessary and may reduce capacity. Desorption <10% is from a single CaCl2 release step, not repeated regeneration or destruction. No actual wastewater, column, economic or life-cycle analysis is reported.
Action required: Separate raw-clay results from activated derivatives in the processing–cost–performance framework. Report the concentration range and matrix (artificial aqueous solutions) alongside removal; do not claim field/trace performance. Treat low desorption as retention only. Keep EC units as published pending source verification and note that supplementary data were not provided.

Paper: Nguyen et al. (2025) — progress in biochar-derived adsorbents for antibiotic wastewater remediation
Critical caveat for synthesis: This is a review, not a primary experiment. Table 3 (PDF p. 24) compiles qmax from many separate studies under non-harmonized conditions and includes a bisphenol A (BPA) entry within an antibiotic-focused capacity table. The review also discusses modification methods that may generate acidic/alkaline or metal-containing wastes and notes the risks of residual PAHs, phenolics and metals and unresolved spent-adsorbent safety. No standardized process cost, yield, energy inventory or cross-material LCA is reported.
Action required: Use for preparation/modification taxonomy, mechanism discovery and identifying primary studies. Do not rank its compiled qmax values without tracing each original study, checking units, mass balance and endpoint. Keep treatment burden and spent-media risks explicit; treat proposed sustainability advantages as hypotheses unless quantified.

Paper: Singh, Vinayagam & Selvaraj (2026) — activated carbon and biochar for tetracycline removal
Critical caveat for synthesis: The review is restricted to tetracycline and searches only Scopus and Google Scholar using a Boolean query that requires the terms activated carbon AND biochar AND tetracycline AND adsorption AND biomass. This can miss relevant studies that focus on only AC or only BC, or that do not use all terms in indexed fields. Its secondary capacity examples are not standardized; one cited Schizochytrium-derived biochar example reports a Langmuir-estimated 1357.5 mg/g while the same paragraph says Freundlich described the equilibrium data better. The paper calls for more real wastewater, repeated regeneration, metal-leaching, pilot-scale, TEA and LCA work.
Action required: Use as a recent TC-specific synthesis and discovery source only. Verify any high qmax against the original data and mass balance, and preserve the discrepancy between model fit and reported Langmuir estimate. Do not generalize its TC-only findings to all antibiotics or treat review examples as independent measurements.

Paper: Ajala et al. (2023) — biomass/biochar-based adsorption of antibiotic pollutants
Critical caveat for synthesis: This is a broad review, not a primary experiment. Its Table 6 compiles different antibiotics, sorbents, initial concentrations, doses, times, pH values, temperatures, capacity metrics and removal percentages. The conclusion explicitly notes that most reviewed work used synthetic aqueous systems and that spent sorbent/residual antibiotic fate was rarely described. It also notes environmental and cost concerns from chemical modifiers. The review warns that high COD removal does not necessarily establish high antibiotic removal.
Action required: Use for taxonomy, literature discovery, regeneration and fixed-bed context. Check original primary studies before using numerical performance claims; keep removal%, observed uptake, fitted qmax, column capacity, COD removal and degradation as distinct endpoints. Include real-water matrix and spent-media safety gaps in our synthesis.

Paper: Liu et al. (2025) — kaolin–alginate beads for chlortetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: Primary study batch tests used 20–100 mg/L CTC. SPE and continuous-column demonstrations used 5 mg/L CTC-spiked distilled/tap/river water, not ambient trace-level contamination. KN@Alg PSO-calculated qe (144.307 mg/g) is much higher than experimental qe (68.700 mg/g; PSO R²=0.838), whereas PFO qe is closer. Four regeneration cycles are short-term evidence. Reported cost (0.095 US$/g) assumes four cycles and cites an unusual electricity price unit of US$/g; it is not a full TEA/LCA.
Action required: Keep observed qe, fitted qmax and column outcomes separate. Describe dynamic tests as 5 mg/L spiked-water matrix. Preserve the kinetic-fit discrepancy and verify the stated electricity-cost unit/calculation before citing cost estimates.

Paper: Maged et al. (2020) — acid-activated bentonite for ciprofloxacin
Critical caveat for synthesis: The NB comparator was purified using acetate/acetic acid at pH≈5, H2O2, NaCl and repeated water washing before AAB was produced with 0.5 M HCl. Batch tests used synthetic mg/L CIP solutions. NaCl from 0 to 0.5 M reduced removal from 59.8% to 16.1% for NB and 95.3% to 75.5% for AAB. The fixed-bed first-cycle qbed was 97.12 mg/g but removal was 37.99%. Table 6 cycle qbed values 97.12, 61.85 and 28.14 mg/g sum to 187.11 mg/g, while the conclusion states 178.11 mg/g.
Action required: Describe NB as lab-purified, AAB as additionally acid-activated; account for washing/heating/acid inputs in the continuum. Keep batch qmax separate from column qbed and flag the 187.11 vs 178.11 mg/g discrepancy. Note salt sensitivity and moderate first-cycle column removal.

Paper: Hamid et al. (2025) — waste-based biochar adsorbents for antibiotic pollution
Critical caveat for synthesis: The review reports finding 88 articles from 2004–2024 through a Google Scholar assessment, but the inspected method does not present a reproducible PRISMA-style systematic search flow. Its tables compile differing source studies, conditions, endpoints and units, so they are not standardized performance comparisons. It highlights high-concentration batch bias, capacity loss on regeneration, regeneration energy/cost and secondary waste, and limited real-water/pilot testing.
Action required: Use as a supporting review and literature-discovery source. Trace numerical examples to primary papers before ranking and verify units and endpoints. Treat claims of low cost/energy/sustainability as qualitative unless supported by quantified process inventory or LCA.

Paper: Liang et al. (2024) — NiFe2O4/biochar composite for tetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: The high reported Langmuir qmax (420.41 mg/g) is a fitted value from synthetic aqueous TC tests. The article reports 93.9% removal at 1 g/L and 20 mg/L TC, but no actual wastewater or fixed-bed validation. Humic acid and Ca/Mg salts suppress removal, and after four cycles removal remains about 72%. Preparation requires 700°C pyrolysis, nickel/iron salts, concentrated ammonia to pH≈11, 180°C/12 h hydrothermal treatment, repeated water/ethanol washing and vacuum drying. No full cost/LCA or Ni/Fe leaching analysis is provided; supplementary tables containing full model parameters are absent from uploaded PDF.
Action required: Keep qmax, removal percentage and reuse retention separate; do not rank on fitted qmax alone. Include metal-salt/ammonia/heating/washing burden and ion/organic-matter interference. Before making feasibility claims, require leaching, spent-regeneration-liquid, real-water and process-cost evidence.

Paper: Pinheiro et al. (2024 preprint) — amoxicillin adsorption by chitosan and alginate beads
Critical caveat for synthesis: The uploaded PDF is the Research Square preprint v1, not the full published journal PDF. A check of the published abstract and ResearchGate publisher preview on 2026-10-27 confirms the headline optimum pH 4 and capacities (alginate 74.2±0.3 mg/g; chitosan 80.4±0.2 mg/g using 1 g adsorbent), but does not verify the complete published methods, fitted isotherm parameters, kinetic diffusion asymptotes or thermodynamic tables. The source prepares separate chitosan and alginate beads, rather than a mixed composite. Tests are high concentration (300 mg/L for pH optimization; isotherms 50–300 mg/L). The text reports alginate uptake 71.3 mg/g, while Table 2 gives fitted Weber–Morris q∞ 136.75±8.2 mg/g. The paper generally says Freundlich fits better despite Langmuir qmax estimates. Alginate reportedly dissolves above pH 6. Active ingredient was sourced from a commercial capsule; excipient/assay controls are not fully clear in inspected preprint methods.
Action required: Use the published abstract only for the headline pH/capacity claim. Keep detailed preprint tables/model extraction provisional until the published full text/supplement is checked. Distinguish measured kinetic uptake from fitted diffusion asymptotes and from Langmuir qmax. Note narrow pH operability, high-concentration synthetic-water tests, and absence of real-water, regeneration, cost and LCA data.

Paper: Sousa et al. (2025) — chitosan-based materials in antibiotic interactions, in vitro/in silico overview
Critical caveat for synthesis: This is a supporting overview focused on tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, cephalexin and azithromycin, not a primary experiment. Tables 2–3 compile capacities from heterogeneous primary papers and are not standardized rankings. The inspected method does not present a PRISMA-style reproducible study-selection flow. Crosslinking can improve mechanics but consume amino adsorption sites; some crosslinkers have toxicity concerns. DFT/docking models simplify real aqueous interfaces and depend on selected protonation state, model size and solvent treatment.
Action required: Use for taxonomy and citation discovery; trace numerical data and specific mechanism claims to the cited primary paper. Do not mix review-derived capacities into the primary-study database rankings or treat computed binding energies as direct evidence of real-water treatment performance. Preserve crosslinker toxicity, site blockage and regeneration as trade-offs.

Paper: Shi et al. (2024) — nano-clay montmorillonite for tetracycline
Critical caveat for synthesis: Methods specify 0.03 g clay in 50 mL TC solution (0.6 g/L), while the conclusion gives optimal dosage as 0.03 g/L. Reported maximum-related values differ: 500 mg/g in the results discussion, 526 mg/g in abstract/conclusion and fitted Langmuir qm=558.184 mg/g. If C0=120 mg/L and 0.03 g in 50 mL apply to the same >90% removal/526 mg/g statement, initial TC mass is 6 mg and the maximum observed uptake is 200 mg/g. The text may be mixing equilibrium concentration and initial concentration, so conditions require reconciliation. Prep uses HCl, ethanol/butyl acetate, heating, filtration and washing; no product yield/cost, solvent recovery, actual wastewater/column, regeneration or LCA is reported.
Action required: Keep fitted qmax, observed uptake and percentage removal distinct. Preserve the dose and concentration-label mismatch. Do not use 500/526/558.184 mg/g in comparative rankings until the source's precise conditions and mass balance are reconciled. Classify as treated nano-clay, not entirely untreated clay.

Paper: Mangla et al. (2022) — critical review on adsorptive removal of antibiotics
Critical caveat for synthesis: Publisher preview and PubMed metadata are accessible, but the full text was not accessible from public pages inspected in this session. Abstract indicates a broad review of biochar, biopolymers, CNTs, clays, MOFs, microalgae, adsorption mechanisms, kinetics/isotherms, regeneration and cost. Detailed tables and primary citations have not been full-text verified in this corpus. The abstract makes broad comparative statements that should not be reused uncritically without checking methods and source-study conditions.
Action required: Keep FULLTEXT-NEEDED despite reviewing metadata/abstract. Do not extract detailed numerical tables or treat abstract conclusions as fully screened evidence. Obtain the article from legitimate institutional access or an author-accepted version before final retain/exclude decision. Track Q1 separately from full-text status.

Paper: Saya et al. (2023) — mGG/GO for CIP
Critical caveat for synthesis: Publisher and author-posted SSRN abstracts confirm author-reported maximum adsorption capacity555.56mg/g and Langmuir/PSO model hierarchy. Third-party Scribd 14-page mirror gives Table2 Langmuir fitted qmax555.56mg/g,KL=.0173L/mg,R²=.9915, while prose saysR²=.9989 (regression form not mapped); kinetic PSO fitted qe38.7596mg/g,R²=.9961 and PFO26.15mg/g,R²=.8544. For baseline, feed ceiling≈1,988mg/g; at700mg/L/10mL/5mg it is1,400mg/g; if5g/L/10mL is used it is140mg/g, making qmax555.56 impossible on that same run. SSRN 27-page author-preprint page links final article but PDF delivery fails; publisher full text gated. No normalized cost/yield/energy or real-water test.
Action required: Keep qmax and fitted kinetic qe separate; disclose the10× dose discrepancy and mixed provenance. Do not rank until full official text or author data clarifies isotherm dose and regression statistics. Cite publisher abstract for headline capacity/model claims; use Scribd details only as explicitly provisional mirror evidence.

Critical caveat for synthesis: Primary abstract confirms Langmuir-fitted q_m=1233mg/g at313K, PSO kinetics, spontaneous/endothermic adsorption, slight pH effect, NaCl facilitation above0.001M and slight humic-acid inhibition. Full primary isotherm range, C0/dose/V, fit statistics, observed qe and regeneration cycles inaccessible. Action required: Use q_m only as a model-derived abstract endpoint, not measured qe or quantitative winner. Quarantine review-table condition vectors; verify primary full text before condition-labelled comparison.

Paper: Ghadim et al. (2013) — GO for TC
Critical caveat for synthesis: PLOS full text confirms GO–TC batch and release study. Isotherm Table2 Langmuir fitted q_m=322.43±1.25mg/g(298K),101.87±1.08(303K),73.53±.55(308K), while D–R fitted q_m=24.62±.74,22.92±.59,24.94±.61mg/g; these are model parameters, not observed qe. Paper: Choi & Choi (2022) — GO/Ca-alginate/PAM beads for CIP
Critical caveat for synthesis: Primary MDPI/PMC full text: q_m=6.846mg/g is Langmuir-fitted, not observed q_e. Paper: Wu et al. (2013) — GO/calcium-alginate fibers for CIP
